title: The Story of the Bicycle
description: How the bicycle developed from a wooden toy into a machine that changed society.
instructions: Read the passage about the history of the bicycle, then choose the best answer for each question.

paragraphs.text: The bicycle is so common today that it is easy to forget it was once a strange new invention. One of the earliest versions appeared in Germany in the early nineteenth century. It was made of wood and had no pedals, so riders had to push it along the ground with their feet. People called it a 'running machine', and for a short time it was a fashionable toy for wealthy young men.

Later in the century, inventors added pedals to the front wheel. To make the bicycle go faster, some designers made the front wheel enormous and the back wheel very small. These machines, often called 'penny-farthings', could reach high speeds, but they were difficult to climb onto. If the rider hit a stone or stopped suddenly, he could easily fall over the top and be badly hurt.

The real breakthrough came in the 1880s with the 'safety bicycle'. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel. Soon afterwards, air-filled rubber tyres made riding much more comfortable on rough roads. This design was so successful that most modern bicycles still look very similar to it.

The safety bicycle quickly changed people's lives. For the first time, ordinary workers could travel several miles to a job without paying for a horse or a train ticket. The bicycle also gave many women a new sense of freedom, and it even influenced fashion, as women began to wear more practical clothes for riding. More than a century later, the bicycle remains one of the cheapest and most efficient ways to travel.

The bicycle also influenced other inventions. Building bicycles required light frames, strong wheels and well-made chains, and many of these skills were later used to build the first cars and aircraft. In fact, the Wright brothers, who made one of the first powered flights in 1903, ran a bicycle shop before they built their famous plane. Cyclists also played a part in changing the roads themselves. In several countries, they were among the first groups to demand smoother, better-kept roads, which later benefited drivers too.

During the twentieth century, however, the bicycle faced a powerful rival. As cars became cheaper, many families in Europe and North America chose to drive instead of cycle, and towns were redesigned around motor traffic. In other parts of the world, the story was different. In China and the Netherlands, for example, bicycles remained the main way of getting around for millions of people for many decades. In these places, the bicycle was not a hobby but an ordinary part of daily life.

Today's bicycles are very different from the wooden running machine. Frames are made from light metals or carbon fibre, gears make it easier to climb hills, and mountain bikes can ride over rocks and mud. Cycling is also a major sport: famous races such as the Tour de France, first held in 1903, attract huge crowds every year. Most recently, electric bikes have brought cycling to people who once thought it was too hard. Two hundred years after its invention, the bicycle is still finding new riders.
